title: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Application and Support
subtitle: The rulebook for the application-layer software every Internet host must run: Telnet, FTP, TFTP, mail, DNS and start-up.
summary: RFC 1123 is the application-layer half of the Host Requirements standard, written to pair with RFC 1122. It does not invent new protocols. It takes the existing ones (Telnet, FTP, TFTP, SMTP, DNS, boot-time configuration and network management), corrects their errors and says exactly what a host MUST, SHOULD or MAY do. Its best-known line is the robustness principle: be liberal in what you accept and conservative in what you send.

eli5.summary: Lots of people built computers that were supposed to talk to each other, but each one followed the rules a little differently. This is a big checklist that says which rules everyone must follow and which are only good ideas, so all the computers can understand each other.

tldr.problem: Early Internet application software, written by many vendors from loosely worded specifications, often failed to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: One document walks through Telnet, FTP, TFTP, SMTP, DNS, host initialization and management, fixing errors and labelling each requirement MUST, SHOULD or MAY.
tldr.outcome: Its checklists, timeouts and the robustness principle became the common baseline for host software, though many of its protocol details have since been replaced.

lineage.title: Host requirements and the protocols they cover

today: RFC 1123 is still listed as an Internet Standard and is part of STD 3, but much of its detail has been overtaken. SMTP is now specified in RFC 5321, which updates this document, and the DNS-over-TCP rules in section 6.1.3.2 were revised by RFC 7766 and RFC 9210. Few people read it end to end now. Its influence lives on in the habits it taught: per-command timeouts and exponential backoff in network code, logging odd protocol events, treating enumerations as open-ended, and the robustness principle, which is still quoted in protocol design discussions, though not without argument about whether being liberal in what you accept has its own costs.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC is one of a pair. Its companion, RFC 1122, covers the communication layers (link, IP and transport); this one covers the application and support protocols above them. Together they were meant to guide vendors, implementors and users of Internet software, and the editor describes them as the consensus of a large body of technical experience.

The document enumerates the standard protocols a host must use and incorporates the existing specifications by reference. It then corrects their errors and adds guidance. The RFC admits that its list of requirements is incomplete by itself, since the full set is in the underlying protocol documents. Many of its "requirements" are already implied elsewhere; they are repeated because "some past implementation has made the wrong choice".

Each requirement carries one of three levels. MUST is absolute. SHOULD allows valid reasons to differ if the implications are understood. MAY is truly optional. An implementation that meets every MUST is conditionally compliant; one that also meets every SHOULD is unconditionally compliant.

MUST
An absolute requirement. Failing it makes an implementation non-compliant.
SHOULD
Recommended. Ignore it only for good reason and with the consequences weighed.
MAY
Truly optional. One vendor may include it and another omit it.
sections.eli5: Think of a rulebook for a big game with many players. Some rules are "you absolutely must", some are "you really ought to", and some are "if you like". The book also fixes places where the old rules were confusing.

sections.title: General principles and issues
sections.content:
Before any single protocol, the RFC gives advice that applies at every layer. The best known is the robustness principle: "Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send." Software should be written to deal with every conceivable error, and should assume the network contains hosts that send packets designed to have the worst effect. An enumeration of values, such as error codes, must be assumed incomplete: if a specification defines four error codes, the software must not break when a fifth shows up.

The second half matters too. Other hosts may have bugs, so it is unwise to rely on legal but obscure features.

Section 1.2 also asks for error logging that records strange protocol events (preferably counting abnormalities and exposing the counts to management) without flooding disks, and for configurable parameters with defaults that follow the official protocol, not workarounds for faulty systems.

Section 2 adds concrete rules. A host name may begin with a letter or a digit. A host MUST handle names of up to 63 characters and SHOULD handle up to 255. Applications MUST cope with soft DNS errors and wait a reasonable interval between retries. They MUST set a configurable Type-of-Service value, and a multihomed host should try each of a remote host's addresses in turn.

Section 2.1 tells software to check for a dotted-decimal address such as 192.0.2.1 before doing a DNS lookup, since a valid host name can never have that form: its last label is alphabetic.
sections.eli5: The golden rule is: be kind when you listen and careful when you speak. If someone says something a bit odd, do not fall over. When you talk, say it in the plainest way so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: Remote login: Telnet
sections.content:
Telnet, specified in RFC 854, links a user's keyboard and display to a command interpreter on another machine over one TCP connection. Its default data stream is the Network Virtual Terminal (NVT): 7-bit ASCII with escape sequences for control functions. RFC 1123 walks through the specification and fixes the places that caused trouble.

Every implementation MUST include option negotiation, and a host MUST refuse an unsupported option by replying WONT or DONT to a DO or WILL. If all negotiation fails, it MUST fall back to an NVT. The Go-Ahead function, built for half-duplex terminals, is largely vestigial: a server that never sends GA MUST attempt to negotiate Suppress Go Ahead.

The longest discussion is about the end-of-line convention, which the RFC calls "a massive and continuing interoperability headache". Telnet defines CR LF as end-of-line, but RFC 854 was ambiguous about what a client should send when the user presses Enter, and some clients sent CR NUL. The fix is on the server side: on an ASCII server, CR LF and CR NUL MUST have the same effect. A User Telnet MUST be able to send CR LF, CR NUL or LF, with CR LF the recommended default.
sections.eli5: Telnet lets you type on one computer and have it act like a keyboard on another. Two people may press "Enter" in slightly different ways, so the rule is that the listener must understand both ways.

sections.title: File transfer: FTP and TFTP
sections.content:
For FTP (RFC 959), the RFC corrects ambiguities and defines a minimum implementation that every server and user program MUST support: ASCII non-print, IMAGE and LOCAL 8 types, Stream mode, and a list of 26 commands from USER and PASS to RETR, STOR, LIST, PASV and QUIT. Servers MUST implement PASV. A server SHOULD have a configurable idle timeout of at least 5 minutes, and when choosing between a 4xx and 5xx reply it SHOULD send 4xx if the failure might clear up within hours. A client should base decisions only on the first digit of a reply code.

TFTP is the small cousin used for booting from a ROM. Section 4.2.3.1 documents a serious bug in its specification, the "Sorcerer's Apprentice Syndrome": if one ACK is delayed and a packet is retransmitted, both sides keep answering each duplicate with a duplicate of their own, so every packet is sent twice for the rest of the transfer. The fix, which implementations MUST include, is that the sender must never resend the current DATA packet on receiving a duplicate ACK. TFTP MUST also use an adaptive timeout, with at least exponential backoff.

TFTP has weak access control. A server SHOULD allow configurable restrictions on pathnames, and a TFTP request sent to a broadcast address SHOULD be silently ignored.
sections.eli5: FTP is like sending a package through a post office with a long list of counter rules. TFTP is a tiny version for when you can only carry a very small bag. It had a bug where both people kept repeating themselves to each other, and the fix is: do not repeat yourself just because you heard an echo.

sections.title: Electronic mail: SMTP and RFC 822
sections.content:
The mail section revises RFC 821 (SMTP) and RFC 822 (message format). It separates the envelope, which SMTP carries with the MAIL and RCPT commands, from the message, which is a header and body. A receiver MUST implement VRFY and SHOULD implement EXPN, though they MAY be disabled by configuration.

Several rules discourage old habits. Senders SHOULD NOT use explicit source routes such as @ALPHA,@BETA:joe@GAMMA; the plain address user@domain should always suffice, with MX records handling the cases where routing once seemed necessary. A receiver MUST still accept the syntax, and without relay support SHOULD try delivering straight to the host after the right-most @. A receiver MAY check the HELO name but MUST NOT refuse mail because the check fails.

The larger part concerns reliability. Mail that cannot be sent immediately MUST be queued and retried. The retry interval SHOULD be at least 30 minutes and the give-up time at least 4 to 5 days. When accepting a message with a 250 reply after DATA, a receiver takes responsibility for it and MUST NOT lose it. A sender MUST be able to try each address from the MX and multihomed lists in order, and SHOULD try at least two. Mailers MUST handle messages of at least 64K bytes.
sections.eli5: Mail between computers is like passing a letter along a chain. If the next person is not home, you keep the letter and try again later, for days if needed. Once someone says "I've got it", they must not lose it.

sections.title: Name service: the Domain Name System
sections.content:
Section 6.1 says every host MUST implement a DNS resolver and use it to convert names to addresses and back. A host MAY also keep a local host table, as an extra source and not a replacement. The RFC explains why: the old central host table grew too large to update and distribute in time, which is why the DNS was invented.

Most of the rules protect the shared system from careless clients. A resolver MUST bound the effort spent on one request and, after several retransmissions with no answer, give up and return a soft error. Retries SHOULD use exponential backoff, and implementations SHOULD cache both temporary failures and negative answers. Zero-TTL records MUST be returned to the client but not cached.

Ordinary (non-zone-transfer) queries MUST first be sent over UDP. If the answer is truncated and TCP is supported, the requester SHOULD retry over TCP. TCP MUST be used for zone transfers. A mailer must not use a truncated MX answer, since that could create mail loops. The RFC notes that the 512-byte UDP limit means future record types may need TCP, a point later RFCs strengthened.

The WKS record type is mentioned only to say that applications SHOULD NOT depend on it. To confirm a service is present, simply try to use it.
sections.eli5: The Domain Name System is a giant phone book that turns a name like a website into a number. The rules say: ask politely, do not keep shouting if nobody answers, and remember answers (including "no such name") for a while so you do not pester the book.

sections.title: Host initialization and remote management
sections.content:
For a diskless host, starting up has two phases: first configure the IP layer (at least the host's own address and the boot server's address, plus an address mask and default gateways to boot across a router), then load the system code over the network using a file transfer protocol.

Section 6.2.2.1 reviews the options. ICMP Information Request/Reply is obsolete and useful only if the host already knows its host number. RARP (RFC 903) maps a link-layer address to an IP address but does not cross gateways, so it needs a server on every network and supplies nothing else. ICMP Address Mask messages give the mask. BOOTP (RFC 951) supplies the host and server addresses and a boot file name, with optional mask and gateways. The RFC recommends BOOTP with the vendor extensions of RFC 1084, and TFTP for the loading phase, though not to a broadcast address.

Section 6.3 asks that a host SHOULD include a management agent for either SNMP or CMOT, and that each protocol module SHOULD implement the relevant variables in the standard Management Information Base. A managed host must implement the System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP and UDP groups. Some values are fixed for hosts: icmpOutRedirects MUST always be zero, since hosts do not send Redirects.
sections.eli5: A computer with no memory of its own wakes up asking "who am I, and where do I get my instructions?" First it finds out its address, then it downloads its instructions. The rest of the section says grown-up computers should also let an administrator peek in to check on them.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
RFC 1123 is candid about its limits here. Its Security Considerations section says there are "many security issues in the application and support programs of host software", but that a full discussion is beyond the scope of the RFC. It points to the places where security comes up: TFTP (sections 4.2.1, 4.2.3.4 and 4.2.3.5), the SMTP VRFY and EXPN commands (5.2.3), HELO (5.2.5) and DATA (5.2.8).

In practice that means a handful of rules. TFTP offers no access control of its own, so servers should restrict which pathnames can be used and ignore broadcast requests, because directed broadcasts to random networks could be a significant security hole. VRFY and EXPN are used to diagnose mail delivery problems, but some see EXPN as a privacy or even security exposure, so both may be disabled by configuration. A HELO check on the sender's name may be useful but must not be a reason to reject mail.

More generally, the robustness principle in section 1.2.2 tells implementors to assume that the network is full of hostile hosts and to design defensively. That was written in 1989; today's threat landscape, and the use of encryption and authentication, are far outside what this document addresses.
sections.eli5: The authors say plainly: "there are lots of ways bad people could cause trouble, and we cannot cover them all here." They point out a few risky spots and tell everyone to expect that some computers on the network are up to no good.

items.title: Robustness principle
items.text: Be liberal in what you accept, and conservative in what you send.

items.title: Enumerations are open
items.text: If a specification defines four error codes, software must not break when a fifth shows up.

items.title: Log strange events
items.text: Count abnormalities, log selectively, and avoid filling disks with harmless noise.

items.title: Defaults follow the standard
items.text: Parameters are configurable, but built-in defaults should implement the official protocol, not workarounds for faulty systems.

messages.label: ACK X
messages.note: Delayed in the network, so A times out.

messages.label: ACK X again
messages.note: B answers the duplicate with a duplicate.

messages.label: DATA X+1
messages.note: The delayed first ACK X arrives.

messages.label: DATA X+1 again
messages.note: The second ACK X arrives and A resends the current packet.

messages.label: ACK X+1 again
messages.note: From here every packet is duplicated. The fix: never resend current DATA on a duplicate ACK.
